home.title: GPU Unlock — which NVIDIA cards are supported, and the measured numbers
home.description: The accepted PCI device IDs for the GPU Unlock kernel modules, and the same-card stock-vs-unlocked measurements on RTX 4090, RTX 4070 Ti SUPER and RTX 2080 Ti. The build and install walkthrough is on gpu-unlock.com.
home.h1: Which cards the SM speed-select override accepts, and what it measured
home.lead: Three upstream kernel modules unlock the tensor throughput NVIDIA reserves for other parts of the chip. This site is the evidence side of the project: the accepted device IDs, how well each card is actually known, and the before-and-after numbers measured on the same card. How to build and install the module is on gpu-unlock.com.
home.statIdsNote: Across AD102, GA102, GA103, GA104 and GA106 from the merged Ampere/Ada module, plus TU102, TU104 and TU106 from the separate Turing module. Acceptance is not the same as a confirmed card — see the card list.
home.statMeasuredNote: RTX 4090, RTX 4070 Ti SUPER and RTX 2080 Ti. Everything else rests on user reports or is untested.
home.statGainNote: f16/f32 and bf16/f32 on RTX 4090. FP32 and INT8 were never rate-limited and do not move.
home.whatBody: The module enables the SM speed-select override before the stock NVIDIA driver binds. It runs from the initramfs, so the driver never sees the card in its stock state. What it changes is the tensor rate limit; the core SM clock and the raster pipeline are untouched.
home.whatWarnTitle: Hardware risk is real and documented
home.whatWarnBody: The unlock writes speed-select registers and performs an FLR before the driver loads. Keep an unmodified stock boot entry, validate one cold boot before making anything persistent, and read the Turing module's own warning about sustained tensor power draw before you enable it on an RTX 20 series card.
home.benchBody: Every row below compares stock and unlocked on the same card with the same binary. Modes that were already at full rate are omitted here and shown in full on the benchmarks page.
home.seeAllBench: All benchmark rows, including the paths that did not change

statusExplain.measured: A fork published stock-vs-unlocked numbers from one card with the same binaries.
statusExplain.reported: Someone filed a compatibility report. The forks did not independently revalidate it.
statusExplain.partial: The override applies but tensor throughput stays where it was.
statusExplain.untested: The module accepts the device ID. Nobody has published a result.
statusExplain.unsupported: Deliberately not in the accepted list.

gpus.idsTitle: How to check your own card
gpus.idsBody: Run `lspci -nn | grep -i nvidia` and match the `10de:xxxx` device ID against the accepted list below. GeForce and CMP GA102/GA104 IDs are in the accepted list; professional RTX A-series and data-centre parts are not. AD102 accepts only the RTX 4090, and AD103 is limited to the exact RTX 4070 Ti SUPER canary address. The Turing IDs (TU102, TU104, TU106) are accepted by a separate module, so a Turing card needs the Turing install, not the merged one.

device.benchNote: Same card, same binary, stock versus unlocked. Modes that did not change are reported too — an unlock that does not move a path is a fact worth having.
device.noBench: No same-card measurement has been published for this card. Its status comes from user compatibility reports, not from a benchmark run under the maintainers' control.
device.familyRef: No same-card run exists for this board. The nearest measured card on the same unlock module is {name} ({family}); its gains are a reference point, not this card's numbers.
device.familyNone: This board belongs to the {family} generation, which has {total} boards listed here and not one same-card measurement. Nothing on this site should be read as its expected gain.
device.cutlassNote: A different program from the loop above: one 4096³ kernel timed by the CUTLASS profiler, reported in GFLOP/s. Kept in its own table because the two numbers do not share a method.
device.peakLine: Peak gain {peak}× on this card in this group.

bench.title: Benchmarks: stock versus unlocked
bench.description: Every same-card stock-vs-unlocked measurement published by the GPU Unlock Ada fork, including the tensor modes that did not change and the FP8 CUTLASS pair that measured 1.0029×.
bench.methodBody: The RTX 4090 rows come from a register-resident MMA issue-rate loop run at 20,000 iterations and three repetitions per mode, best-of-three reported. The RTX 4070 Ti SUPER rows come from the fork's tensor-modes-comparison.json, 66 SMs, driver 580.178.04, 240 W cap, 20,000 iterations and three repetitions, with all-one inputs across eight independent chains. The FP8 pair is a separate CUTLASS 4.8.1 profiler run on one sm_89 kernel.
bench.fp8Title: The FP8 pair that did not move
bench.fp8Body: The fork measured a matched E4M3 FP8 input, FP32 accumulate 4096³ GEMM on the 4070 Ti SUPER with the same CUTLASS profiler binary, one kernel, 10 warmups and 20 profiling iterations, requiring device-reference verification. Both runs passed their reference checks.
bench.readTitle: How to read a ratio of 1.00×
bench.readBody: A 1.00× row is not a failed unlock. It says that particular path was never rate-limited, so the override had nothing to restore. If you benchmark your own card and see 1.00× on the mode you care about, the unlock may well have applied correctly and simply does not help that workload.

explorer.emptyBody: Try a mode name like bf16, or clear the filter.

modes.tableTitle: Every card measured on this mode
modes.tableNote: Same card, same driver, same binary. The unlocked figure is the only variable.
modes.coverageBody: Only cards with a same-card measurement on this mode appear in the table. A card missing from it has not been measured on this path, which is not the same as failing.

tensor-f16-f16.name: FP16 with an FP16 accumulator
tensor-f16-f16.body: The full-rate tensor-core path. On Ada this is already at the hardware limit before any unlock, so a measured 1.02× is best-of-three noise rather than a gain.

tensor-f16-f32.name: FP16 with an FP32 accumulator
tensor-f16-f32.body: The shape most inference kernels use. This is the path the SM speed-select fuse rate-limits on Ada, which is why an unlock doubles it.

tensor-bf16-f32.name: BF16 with an FP32 accumulator
tensor-bf16-f32.body: Same rate-limit story as FP16/FP32, with BF16's wider exponent. Training and many inference stacks prefer this shape.

tensor-tf32.name: TF32 with an FP32 accumulator
tensor-tf32.body: 19-bit TF32 inputs, aimed at training throughput. Also fuse-gated on Ada, also roughly doubled by the unlock.

tensor-int8.name: INT8 with an INT32 accumulator
tensor-int8.body: Quantized inference. Never rate-limited by the fuse, so the row reads 1.00× and that is the correct result.

tensor-int4.name: INT4 with an INT32 accumulator
tensor-int4.body: The densest quantized path. Like INT8 it was never fuse-gated, so the unlock does nothing here.

tensor-fp8.name: FP8 E4M3 through CUTLASS
tensor-fp8.body: A real GEMM kernel rather than an issue-rate loop. It measured 1.0029×, the clearest single piece of evidence that FP8 was never gated.

dp4a.name: The dp4a integer dot product
dp4a.body: Four INT8 multiply-accumulates per lane. An integer path, so the SM rate fuse leaves it untouched at 1.00×.

fp32-ffma.name: Scalar FP32 fused multiply-add
fp32-ffma.body: The CUDA-core path, not the tensor cores. Included as a control: it holds 1.00× on every card, showing the unlock is scoped to tensor paths.

gemm-f16-f32.name: FP16/FP32 as a cuBLAS GEMM
gemm-f16-f32.body: A different measurement from the issue-rate rows above: a real cuBLAS GEMM at four M.N.K sizes on Turing. Its 1.36–1.64× must not be averaged with the Ada issue-rate numbers.

bench.modesBody: Each card was measured on several instruction paths, and the unlock moves only some of them. Grouping the rows by what they actually exercise keeps a 2.0× on a fused-multiply path from being read as a 2.0× on everything.

install.title: Install GPU Unlock
install.description: The install order that matters: build locally, let the package put gpu_unlock in the initramfs before nvidia, opt in on the kernel command line, and only then make the boot entry persistent.
install.riskBody: The module writes speed-select registers and performs an FLR before the NVIDIA driver binds. Keep a stock boot entry. Validate a cold boot before making anything persistent. The AD103 path is experimental and was validated on one card.
install.verifyBody: The module logs its decisions to the kernel ring buffer. Check the log and confirm the driver bound the card afterwards.
install.disableBody: Remove gpu_unlock.targets= from the kernel command line; for a one-off boot, delete it in the bootloader's edit screen. Removing the packages also removes the module and the initramfs drop-ins.
install.repoAmpere: Ampere: GA102, GA103, GA104, GA106. No Ada support.
install.repoAda: Ada: adds AD102 RTX 4090 and the experimental AD103 canary, and keeps the Ampere device list.
install.repoMerged: Merged: both upstream forks plus the suspend/resume re-unlock path. One clone covers Ampere and Ada.
install.repoTuring: the separate module for RTX 20 series cards, with its own turing_unlock.targets opt-in
install.reqHint: Everything here is checked from the card, not assumed.

windows.title: Windows GPU UNLOCK — the UEFI port for Windows, and what it actually covers
windows.description: impacifist/Windows-GPU-UNLOCK runs the unlock as an EFI payload before Windows boots, instead of as a Linux kernel module. The recorded hardware profiles, the four boot routes, the requirements and the release scope.
windows.h1: The Windows route: an EFI payload that runs before Windows boots
windows.lead: The three projects documented on this site are Linux kernel modules. Windows-GPU-UNLOCK is a different implementation: it installs its own EFI System Partition and performs the register work in a payload that hands off to Windows Boot Manager. It also publishes no stock-vs-unlocked pair, so this page reports the recorded profiles and the boot routes rather than a gain number.
windows.linuxTitle: This is not the Linux module and does not replace it
windows.linuxBody: Nothing here applies to a Linux install, and the kernel module does not apply to Windows. The two share the underlying idea — write the rate-select register before the NVIDIA driver binds — but the boot path, the tooling and the failure modes are different. If you are on Linux, use the card list and the benchmarks on this site.
windows.scopeTitle: What the release is, at the time of writing
windows.scopeBody: The latest tag is {release}, a source-only pre-release. Read the scope list before assuming a card is covered.
windows.cardsBody: A profile covers one card in one specific system. The same GPU model on a different motherboard is not covered by that profile, and only the first row was recorded by the maintainer under their own test.
windows.pathsTitle: Four boot routes, and they are not interchangeable
windows.pathsBody: Which route you take depends on whether the display stays on the discrete card and whether you can use a USB stick. Each has its own guide in the repository.
windows.measureBody: The original B650M / RTX 3090 FE run reported these CUDA 12.6 / cuBLAS 12.6 numbers at 4096 x 4096, as a median of three runs. These are absolute figures from an unlocked card — there is no stock side published for them, so they are not a gain.
windows.teardownTitle: What the recorded run left behind
windows.teardownBody: The successful child reported this state after the unlock, which is the evidence that the card was handed to the driver cleanly.
